background.definition: Somatization is classically defined as the experiencing of psychological distress as physical symptoms. This represents a broad spectrum of presentations from mild medically unexplained symptoms to debilitating symptom complexes involving multiple organ systems. Somatic Symptom Disorder (SSD), as defined by DSM-V criteria (see below), represents the most severe end of the spectrum.

list.listitem: SSD has a 1-year prevalence of 3 in 1000.
Somatization as classically defined above is common, although concrete prevalence data are lacking.
SSD exhibits an approximately 5:1 female to male ratio.
A study of patients presenting with new symptoms found that 36% had clinically significant somatization.
Patients with diagnosed SSD, the severest form of somatization, may generate almost 10 times the medical costs of nonsomatizers.

Somatizing patients with less severe symptomatology still generate 2 times the medical costs as nonsomatizing patients, including unnecessary testing and diagnostic studies, accounting for $265 billion in annual additional expenditures.
Patients with somatization report high levels of disability, particularly related to work.
Physicians can be frustrated by somatization and its failure to respond to medical treatment, straining the physician-patient relationship.
SSD is associated with decreased quality of life, increased functional impairment, and high comorbidity with anxiety and depressive disorders.

Psychological or emotional stress can contribute. For example, in a study of 29 women with somatic symptom disorder and 29 women with depressive disorders, those with a greater number of specific negative psychological factors, (e.g. catastrophizing, negative affectivity, and behavioral avoidance) had a higher intensity of and impairment by somatic symptoms at the same and the next measurement time point in both groups.
Misinterpretation of normal sensations as pathologic leads to increased attention to the symptoms and further amplification.
There may also be a need to assume the sick role.
The physical symptoms may be a method of expressing emotional distress when the patient cannot do so in words.
The patient does not consciously produce the symptoms, as in factitious disorder or malingering, although sometimes there may be a volitional component.
A systematic review found positive associations between health anxiety and online health information seeking and cyberchondria.

The pathophysiology of somatization is largely unknown, although sensitization or prolonged activation of the brain cytokine system by proinflammatory cytokines may alter brain tryptophan chemistry and contribute to some of the symptomatology of somatization.
An exploratory study observed changes in the glucose metabolism of the caudate and putamen with severe somatization.

One psychoanalytical model of somatization is alexithymia, in which a person has difficulty identifying or describing their emotional and psychological distress, and instead expresses it as physical symptoms.
A systematic review of neuroimaging found morphologic changes in limbic, somatosensory, and motor cortex in patients meeting DSM-IV and DSM-V criteria for somatoform disorders compared with controls.
Consider somatization in patients presenting frequently for multiple vague symptoms. C
Look for evidence of organic pathology in the history, physical examination, and appropriate diagnostic testing. C
Consider use of a validated screening tool such as the PHQ-15. C
Avoid invasive procedures when possible. C
Limit further diagnostic workup once the diagnosis has been established except when there is new evidence or findings of organic pathology. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Distressing, significant disruption of daily life
One or more unexplained physical complaints
Sensory or motor deficits triggered by acute stress
Preoccupation with having a serious illness based on misinterpreted sensations
Intentionally producing symptoms to assume the sick role
Neurologic symptoms, brain lesions on MRI

list.listitem: The DSM-V diagnostic criteria for SSD includes: one or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or result in significant disruption of daily life, excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to the somatic symptoms. The state of being symptomatic is persistent.
The history typically reveals a chronic course of multiple vague symptoms.
The physical examination should not find evidence of organic disease that would account for the symptoms.
Pain or vague sensory deficits may be the only findings, and they are often inconsistent or anatomically inexplicable.
Historically, somatization has been a diagnosis of exclusion.

Consider medical conditions that can cause multiple vague symptoms, including multiple sclerosis, hyperparathyroidism, thyroid disorders, SLE, HIV, and others consistent with a specific presentation, and test or screen appropriately.
Avoid invasive testing unless there is evidence of organic disease, as some of the most serious consequences of somatization are iatrogenic complications.
Once the diagnosis of somatization is established, limit further laboratory testing and radiologic imaging unless there is evidence of organic disease.
The PHQ-15 is a reasonable screening tool for somatiform disorders in primary care.
The SSD-12 is a useful tool in primary care to assess the psychological characteristics associated with somatic symptoms.

It is important to screen for suicidal ideation as somatic symptom disorders are associated with increased risk for suicidal ideation and suicide attempts. In a 2021 systematic review estimates ranged from 24% to 34% of participants who endorsed current active suicidal ideation and 13% to 67% of participants who endorsed a prior suicide attempt.

Tools are available that may help in diagnosis, ranging from simple self-assessment tools such as the PHQ-15 to more complex structured interviews such as the Prime MD. The PHQ-15 is time efficient and has been validated in primary care settings.
When somatization is suspected, consider possible organic etiologies and evaluate when appropriate; then evaluate for common psychiatric comorbidities.
Pursue the diagnosis of somatization when the patient has a typical presentation and no red flags suggest organic pathology ().
Frequent, scheduled visits that focus on the patient's emotional and psychological issues and de-emphasize the physical symptoms are a mainstay of treatment. C
Psychotherapy by a trained mental health professional, especially a cognitive behavioral therapist, may be helpful in improving symptoms for those willing to participate. B
Antidepressants may have a role in treatment of somatization. B
Avoid or limit narcotics for somatized pain. C
There is a high rate of depression and anxiety in somatizing patients; consider treating with antidepressants when depression is present.

A meta-analysis found that antidepressants yielded a substantial improvement in some outcome measures for patients with unexplained symptoms syndromes unrelated to any improvement in mood (NNT = 3). However, the clinical relevance of the improvement is not always clear, and the meta-analysis did not necessarily look at patients with the specific diagnosis of somatization.
Fluoxetine and cognitive behavioral therapy are reasonable treatment options for somatization.
In general, avoid the use of narcotics, benzodiazepines, and other habit-forming medications in patients with somatization.
St. John's wort may be beneficial in the treatment of somatization.
Physical therapy has an uncertain role in the treatment of somatized pain, although it is unlikely to cause harm.
Exercise and relaxation may be beneficial but have not shown a clinically significant benefit in studies.

Psychotherapy by a mental health professional should be attempted if the patient is willing. A systematic review found that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) administered by psychologists is efficacious in somatization.

A systematic review with 15 RCTs and 1671 patients concluded that CBT and behavioral stress management are useful approaches for patients with somatization disorder. CBT improves physical and psychological symptoms as well as disability.

In a multicenter randomized trial with 156 patients with frequent unscheduled visits randomized to remote CBT (phone or videoconference) or treatment as usual, those in the intervention group had improvements in anxiety, depression, and self-assessed overall health.
Internet-Based CBT is superior to psychoeducation, clinical support, and monitoring for anxiety and somatic symptoms.
Guided internet CBT, unguided internet CBT, and bibliotherapy (CBT via book) are equally effective and superior to waitlist control. All are cost-effective.

Therapist-guided internet based CBT (i.e. treatment via a self-help text divided into 12 modules and patient’s communicating with therapists through email) was as efficacious as face-to-face CBT (i.e. 12 weekly in-person sessions and daily homework assignments), for patient’s diagnosed with Somatic Symptom Disorder (n = 116) or Illness Anxiety Disorder/Hypochondriasis (n = 281). The internet based CBT also generated lower net societal costs, including lower therapist costs, potentially reducing a barrier to care.
Brief psychodynamic psychotherapy also demonstrates modest to moderate improvement.

Patients with somatization are often resistant to mental health referrals; reinforce that involvement of such a professional does not mean their symptoms are not "real," but rather that such interventions have demonstrated benefit.
Many psychotherapies and psychosocial interventions show only limited evidence of clinical improvement in somatization when administered by a primary care physician.

Establishing a therapeutic physician-patient relationship and developing coping and symptom management strategies that minimize unnecessary medication and testing are the backbone of treatment for somatization.
Patients with SSD should be seen regularly, ideally prior to the onset or worsening of symptoms so that the patients do not need such symptoms as a reason to see the physician.
Ideally, one establishes and nurtures a therapeutic physician-patient relationship through patient-centeredness, empathy, and adapting one's style to the specific patient's needs.

A simple care recommendation letter to the primary care physician when a patient screened positive for somatization improves patient outcomes. Care recommendations include: brief regularly scheduled appointments, avoiding urgent appointments, minimizing hospitalizations and procedures, view symptoms as part of an unconscious process and do not tell the patient it's "all in your head."

Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) may be an effective treatment option for severe and refractory manifestations of somatization disorder, however this recommendation is based on 5 single case studies, 1 case series, and 1 open trial focusing on the use of ECT.
Psychiatric referral is appropriate for refractory patients, those that request it, and those with severe psychiatric comorbidities.
Medical hospitalization should occur only when there is evidence of organic disease.
Continue to see patients with SSD frequently, even when symptoms are improved. C
Psychodynamic psychotherapy and CBT may result in sustained improvement. B
Somatization tends to be chronic, with the focus of treatment on control and not cure. C

SSD is a chronic condition, frequently lasting into old age. Typically the symptoms wax and wane. Symptoms worsen or new symptoms develop over periods lasting 6 to 9 months concurrent with new or increased stress.
There may be periods of as long as a year of decreased symptomatology.
Less severe forms of somatization may have a milder course, with fewer and less frequent symptoms, although the natural history is less well known.
There are minimal data on the long-term effects of treatment on the course of somatization.
The clinical improvements from CBT and brief psychodynamic psychotherapy have been shown to last for up to 12 months after completion; long-term data are lacking.

In general, the more acute the onset, the more identifiable the stressor, the higher the functioning prior to symptoms, the better the support structure, the fewer the comorbidities, and the briefer the course of symptoms are, the better the prognosis is.
Frequent (every 2-4 wk), scheduled office visits are recommended as part of treatment.
Address the physical symptoms as expressions of emotional distress.
Patients with somatization can develop organic pathology, so utilize an appropriate physical examination during follow-up and use your discretion in the workup of new symptoms.
Be appropriately reassuring; somatization has no direct effect on life expectancy.
Avoid any suggestion that their symptoms are "not real" or "all in their head"; confirm the symptoms' impact and take them seriously.
Cognitively reorient the patient to the notion of controlling the symptoms and their effects, not on curing, and to the relationship of stress with the symptoms.
Inform them that excessive or repeated online health information seeking is associated with health anxiety and older individuals may have even higher rates of anxiety escalation with such searches.
Occasional somatization in children is common.
Recurrent, unexplained somatic symptoms require further examination, and abuse should be considered.
Children with frequent headaches have an increased risk of developing somatization as an adult.
Adolescents hospitalized with somatization related complaints were much more likely to recover if their family accepted the diagnosis as somatization (OR 17.36, p = 0.003).

According to a 2020 systematic review there is a high co-ocurrence of pain and Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders (SSRD) in children (ages 0-17), but rates differ depending on diagnosis and pain location. The high variability in how somatization was defined and measured in questionnaire studies made it difficult to understand the relationship between SSRD and pain, although rates of SSRD diagnoses among pain patients were less frequent than rates of pain amongst SSRD patients.

A study published in 2022 including 67 mother and child dyads showed likely intergenerational transmission of somatoform symptoms, based on maternal report, in the context of maternal post-traumatic stress related to interpersonal violence.
